items.title: Manny Albam interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: And we hung out a lot together, John is a good old friend.

ctx.x: What was a chart going for back then?

Oh it wasn’t going for very much. Copying — I used to copy and Georgie, this is something that really taught me, you asked about books. I didn’t need books. I copied a lot of Georgie’s book. And the arrangers, one of the arrangers was Budd Johnson who © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

was a marvelous tenor player but he wrote a lot of stuff for Earl Hines’ band, Billy Eckstine’s band. And he would bring charts into my room, I had a great room on 52nd Street as a matter of fact. And when he gave me a new score I’d ask him about why he did certain things in the score that I was working on. And he would sit there for hours and tell me what Benny Carter told him and what this guy said about this, and why you put these notes together, it makes the thing ring a little bit more. He, and then later on…

items.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Georgie had a very good book, he was fun to work with, he was a great player himself, we had a lot of good charts, Al Cohn, Manny Albam, Bud Johnson, all kinds of people.

ctx.x: Yeah. So before we get into that too much we skipped Georgie Auld and Alvino Rey.

Yeah well… well Georgie Auld was a fun band to play in, it was kind of, again a real swinging band. Georgie had a very good book, he was fun to work with, he was a great player himself, we had a lot of good charts, Al Cohn, Manny Albam, Bud Johnson, all kinds of people. Fun stuff to play, Georgie was a good guy and then I went with Alvino.
